spatial_claims.claim: Cube ABCDEFGH comprehended in sphere; faces assigned (top ABCD, bottom EFGH, front ABFE, back DCGH, left ADHE, right BCGF); d^2 = 3a^2
Midpoints M_AB, M_BC, M_CD, M_DA placed on edges of each face; midpoints of adjacent edges connected
Each half-edge (midpoint to vertex) divided in extreme and mean ratio; greater segment toward vertex; point N lies on segment from midpoint M_AB to vertex A
Four division points on a face plus the midpoint of an adjacent edge from a neighboring face determine a regular pentagon; all five points lie in one plane
Four pentagon vertices from division points on cube face; fifth vertex is a point raised above or below the face from construction on adjacent face
Twelve pentagonal faces, three meeting at each vertex; 20 vertices, 30 edges
Each vertex of dodecahedron at a definite distance from center O of circumscribing sphere
Each vertex on edge of cube or displaced perpendicular to face; all vertices equidistant from O
All 20 vertices lie on a single sphere centered at O
Side of dodecahedron equals greater segment when edge of cube is cut in extreme and mean ratio (references construction in Steps 3-6 which actually cuts half-edges)

configuration_map: The construction begins with cube ABCDEFGH inscribed in a sphere (Step 1). Each of the 12 edges is bisected (Step 2), giving 12 midpoints on the cube edges. Each half-edge (from midpoint toward vertex, length a/2) is then divided in extreme and mean ratio with the greater segment toward the vertex (Step 3), producing additional points on the cube edges. Each pentagonal face of the dodecahedron uses four of these division points from one cube face plus a fifth point from an adjacent face (Steps 4, 6). The fifth point is described inconsistently as either a midpoint of an adjacent edge (Step 4) or a point raised above/below the face from an adjacent construction (Step 6), but both descriptions place it off the plane of the current cube face. All 20 vertices are claimed equidistant from the center O (Steps 10-13).
pass_reason: The proof makes no mutually contradictory spatial claims. While it contains descriptive vagueness (Steps 4 and 6 give slightly different characterizations of the fifth pentagon vertex) and an algebraic imprecision (Step 15 refers to cutting the full edge rather than the half-edge), these are looseness in argumentation rather than concrete spatial contradictions. There are no angle decomposition errors, no inside/outside contradictions, no ray ordering conflicts, and no cases where the same geometric element is forced into two incompatible positions. The proof is hand-wavy and relies heavily on symmetry, but under the protocol's default presumption of PASS, no specific contradiction can be articulated.
